source: Davidson & Sternberg (1984) The role of insight in intellectual giftedness (ERIC abstract)
finding: Only the abstract is reachable. It names three processes (selective encoding, combination, comparison), notes ways to assess insight, and says an intervention study suggests insight can be trained.
numbers: No sample, N, effect sizes or training gains are given in the abstract. Gifted Child Quarterly 28(2), 58-64.
limits: Full text paywalled; founding numbers still not obtained. Gap 2 stays open.
agent_relevance: Framing only; no founding numbers to cite.

finding: Describes the view as coined by Davidson and Sternberg and lists selective encoding, selective comparison and selective combination. Cites one 1984 book chapter and 'Davidson 1995, 2003'.
numbers: No studies, N or numbers on the page.
limits: Page flags itself as single-source. Not evidence of the effect.
agent_relevance: None beyond naming the three processes.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem (re Davidson 1995 and Aha-accuracy)
finding: Cites Davidson (1995): 12-13% of non-insight problems showed an insight-like warmth pattern. Own data: classic insight problems got more Aha than non-insight in all three experiments, with similar or lower accuracy.
numbers: Recruited N: Exp1 193 (9 removed), Exp1a 82 (8 removed), Exp2 129 (12 removed). Aha-accuracy r for insight problems 0.50, 0.40, 0.495; for non-insight 0.02, 0.24, 0.19. Aha mean difference 10.15, 6.13, 6.13.
limits: The three-process terms do not appear in this paper; it gives only the 12-13% number from Davidson 1995. Analysed N is my subtraction.
agent_relevance: Problem class by label is unreliable; do not route the agent by class. Aha links to correctness mainly on insight-labelled items.

source: uTeBC-NLP (2024) SemEval-2024 Task 9: Can LLMs be lateral thinkers?
finding: Compared direct answering and several chain-of-thought styles on BRAINTEASER sentence puzzles. Plain direct prompts matched or beat CoT for GPT-3.5. Step-structured CoT (Specified-Internal-CoT) was worst. Brief prompts beat long ones.
numbers: Sentence test set 120 items. GPT-3.5 direct 72.5 (compressed) / 75.0 (detailed); Simple-Internal-CoT 70.0/72.5; Specified-Internal-CoT 60.0/62.5; External-CoT 65.0/62.5. With 3-shot retrieval, direct reached 82.5-85.0. GPT-4 direct detailed 95.0, Simple CoT 97.5. Zephyr-7B direct 27.5-32.5; CoT 15.0-42.5.
quote: Models tend to prefer brief and informative prompts over lengthier alternatives.
limits: Sentence puzzles only; one test set; items public (contamination possible); not equal-token. A prescribed multi-step structure hurt GPT-3.5, which is the closest test of gap 1.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence against adding a long fixed step list at the framing stage on weak models. Keep any selective-encoding/combination/comparison step short, and test it against direct answering.

source: SemEval-2024 Task 9 system: iterative CoT prompt optimisation with GPT-4 (arXiv 2405.02517)
finding: Few-shot CoT prompt sets (8 examples) tuned on GPT-4 raised overall BRAINTEASER sentence accuracy over zero-shot, with the biggest gains on adversarial reconstructions.
numbers: GPT-4 zero shot overall 76.7 (adversarial 60.0); multi-shot base 87.5; naive CoT base 85.8; New CoT-Base 87.5; New CoT-Mix 90.0 (adversarial 77.5). Top competition entry 98.3 overall; human 92.0.
limits: Test size not stated (percentages are multiples of 2.5, so about 40 per column; inference). GPT-4 API snapshot Jan-Feb 2024. No formal contamination test; authors read the Mix gain as less memorisation.
agent_relevance: Examples that explain why wrong options fail work better than plain CoT; this resembles a comparison step. Still not an equal-token test.

source: DaVinci at SemEval-2024 Task 9: few-shot prompting GPT-3.5 for unconventional reasoning
finding: Few-shot examples helped much more on word puzzles than sentence puzzles, and two-shot hurt sentence puzzles.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo. Sentence overall: zero-shot 62.6, two-shot 51.7, five-shot 60.8. Word overall: zero-shot 53.5, two-shot 68.6, five-shot 84.4 (Ori&Sem&Con 29.3 to 68.8). Ranks 26th (sentence), 15th (word). No CoT run.
limits: Word-puzzle gains from five examples may reflect pattern learning of the format, not reframing; leaderboard-era data.
agent_relevance: Large gains from surface format examples mean BRAINTEASER word scores overstate reframing ability. Use group-based accuracy.

source: Jiang, Ilievski & Ma (2024) SemEval-2024 Task 9 overview (abstract)
finding: Task had a zero-shot and a fine-tuning setting. Abstract gives participation only.
limits: Abstract only opened; top-score and contamination detail not read here. The 98.3 top sentence score appears in d05.
agent_relevance: Top 98% scores come from systems tuned on the training split, so they are not evidence of zero-shot lateral thinking.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo benchmark (full text, contamination and few-shot sections)
finding: Authors argue memorisation does not explain low scores, because familiar answers should ease endorsement, yet models fail to commit to correct candidates. They admit the riddles are public and propose a rotating set: 42 open items, 159 blind items (includes the 120 human-comparison items), and a post-cutoff private set. A supplementary few-shot test with reasoning demonstrations improved accuracy in all 4 models and significantly in 2; not significant for the top model.
numbers: 201 items, 38 LLMs, zero-shot single attempt. Few-shot detail is in SI Appendix 5, which was not read. A fresh set from children's books not online is under development.
limits: No new uncontaminated set exists yet for BRAINTEASER-type items. No candidate-retention test was run, only a suggestion.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: contamination is argued, not measured. Plan our own held-out items created after the model cutoff.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) Illusion of insight: domain and temperature tables
finding: Spontaneous reasoning shifts hurt in math at every temperature and helped only in cryptic crosswords, where the effect was not significant.
numbers: Math: Qwen2.5-7B 0.661 no-shift vs 0.282 shift; GPT-4o 0.658 vs 0.338; DeepSeek-R1 0.543 vs 0.204; raw temperature gap -18.35 pp (AME -0.083, p about 2.7e-8). Crosswords (Qwen-1.5B): 0.096 vs 0.201, raw +10.54 pp, AME 0.033 p=0.26. Rush Hour about 0. Shift rates 1.2-14%. DeepSeek-R1 shift rate 0-0.25% by temperature.
limits: Only the first 100k of 250k characters read. No riddle or lateral task. Mostly a 1.5B model for the forced cue.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: the wait/aha marker is not a reliable accuracy signal in math and its sign flips by domain. Do not use it as a confidence cue.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) forced reconsideration cue, Table 5
finding: Appending 'Wait, we need to reconsider. Let's think this through step by step.' gave a large gain on math and almost none elsewhere.
limits: Gap 4 stays open for riddles and lateral items: none were tested. Math base accuracy is low, so gains may be correction of sloppy first passes.
agent_relevance: A forced second pass is cheap but domain bound. Test it on lateral items with a fresh set before adding it as an operator.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: CoT lowered accuracy on 3 of 6 tasks chosen because verbal thinking hurts humans (implicit statistical learning, face recognition, data with exceptions). The 3 other tasks showed mixed or no harm. The human mechanisms are verbal overshadowing and over-simple rules.
numbers: Implicit learning (random 50): GPT-4o 87.5 zero-shot vs 64.4 CoT; o1-preview 57.7 vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0 on a 440 subset (-36.3). Faces (random 20): GPT-4o 64.0 vs 51.2; Claude 3 Opus 44.0 vs 29.6. Exceptions, rounds to learn: GPT-4o 2.9 vs 12.5.
limits: Last 44k characters of the page not read. Tasks are not insight problems. Claude 3.5 Sonnet was nearly flat on the learning task (65.9 vs 67.7).
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: the verbalisation-hurts pattern transfers to LLMs on non-insight tasks. Not yet shown for insight items. Supports a budget rule that skips CoT on perceptual or pattern items.

source: Inverse scaling in test-time compute (2025, abstract)
finding: Longer reasoning lowered accuracy on some tasks: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction with constraint tracking. Claude models got more distracted; o-series models overfit to framing.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page; 78-page paper not read.
agent_relevance: Longer traces are not always better; allow early stop and compare with short answers.

source: Macchi, Poli & Caravona (2025) verbalisation and insight: literature as summarised in the paper
finding: Earlier work on verbalisation and insight conflicts. Schooler 1993 found impairment; Fleck & Weisberg (2004, 2013) and Gilhooly et al. (2010) found none; Ball et al. (2015) found thinking aloud similar to silence and suppression helped insight. Macchi & Bagassi (2012) found a drop with concurrent verbalisation.
numbers: Own study N=120 (30 per cell): deer insight 57% silent vs 13% verbalising; cryptarithmetic 30% vs 80%. Interaction beta -3.17, p<0.001, e^beta 0.04 (CI 0.01-0.16).
limits: Same lab as Macchi & Bagassi 2012, so not an outside replication. Earlier studies had 2-3 insight problems (Ball 3, Macchi & Bagassi 2). Gap 9 verbalisation half stays open.
agent_relevance: Do not assume forced verbalisation harms insight items in LLMs; the human evidence is itself mixed.

source: Grimmer, Laukkonen, Tangen & von Hippel (2022) Eliciting false insights with semantic priming
finding: Primed lure anagrams produced false insights that felt like real ones. A second experiment reproduced the effect at a smaller size, and visual similarity added to it.
numbers: Exp1 N=150: false insight rate 0.37 for primed lures vs 0.07-0.09 others; d 1.49-1.73. Aha intensity false 5.81 vs correct 6.12 (d=0.22, N=142). Exp2 N=150: lures 0.13 vs about 0.03, d 1.01-1.09; priming x similarity lure rate 0.24. Intensity false 5.43 vs 6.06 (d=0.35, N=76).
limits: Correct author order is Grimmer first (earlier notes call it Laukkonen 2022). Exp2 is an in-paper replication, same lab; no outside replication cited. Ammalainen and Moroshkina (2021) is called broadly consistent.
agent_relevance: Felt certainty is cheap to induce by priming; primed context can push a model to a confident wrong answer, so keep external checks.

source: Salmon-Mordekovich & Leikin (2023) Insight problem solving is not that special, but business is not quite as usual
finding: Insight problems looked like spatial non-insight problems and unlike verbal ones. Analogical thinking predicted insight best. Secondary tasks hurt only verbal non-insight problems, not insight problems.
numbers: N=115. Divergent thinking explained about 2% of variance. Secondary tasks cut verbal non-insight performance by 29% and 24%. Only about 8% of insight-reported solutions involved an impasse.
limits: One lab; mixed verdict, leaning business-as-usual. It paraphrases Chuderski 2018, Weisberg 2015 and Gilhooly & Murphy 2005 but gives no numbers for them.
agent_relevance: Supports no special insight branch; reframing via analogy-like recall is the lever.

source: Chuderski & Jastrzebski (2018) Much ado about aha (via a search summary, not the paper)
finding: Search summary says 40 insight problems of five types; working memory capacity predicted about 51.8% of insight variance and accounted for about 84.6% of the shared link with reasoning, so insight is little beyond ordinary reasoning plus WM.
numbers: 51.8% and 84.6% are from a catalogue abstract summary, not the paper.
limits: Not opened. Treat as unverified. DeCaro, Van Stockum and Wieth (2017) argue the divergence from their findings comes from excluding participants who knew the solutions, which C&J did not.
agent_relevance: Background only. Gap 8 stays open for this paper.

source: Puzzled by puzzles: when vision-language models can't take a hint (2025, abstract)
finding: Rebus puzzle benchmark (EMNLP 2025 main). VLMs decode simple clues but struggle with abstract reasoning, lateral thinking and visual metaphors.
numbers: No accuracy numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; author list not confirmed here.
agent_relevance: Supports that lateral deficits are not limited to text.
